brief.title: Small wheeled robot
brief.understanding: You want a robot, but haven't said yet what kind or what it should do. I've assumed a small two-wheeled rover you drive from your phone, since that is the simplest and cheapest starting point; the answers below will change the plan if you meant something else (arm, line follower, walker, etc.).

questions.question: What kind of robot do you want?
questions.why: This decides the motors, driver, frame and almost everything else.

questions.question: How should it be controlled?
questions.why: Sets which sensors and which controller are needed.

questions.question: How big should it be?
questions.why: Size sets motor power, battery size and cost.

questions.question: How should it be powered?
questions.why: Determines run time, weight and charging circuitry.

questions.question: What is your budget for parts for one robot?
questions.why: Limits the choice of motors, sensors and chassis.

requirements: Chassis about 15-20 cm long, total weight under 500 g
Two driven wheels plus one caster; top speed about 0.5 m/s on flat indoor floors
Powered by 2 x 18650 cells in series (7.4 V nominal, about 2000-2600 mAh)
Run time at least 60 minutes of continuous driving
Controlled from a phone over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth, range at least 10 m indoors
Motor driver rated for at least 1 A continuous per motor
Power switch and low-battery cutoff or warning at about 6.4 V

blocks.name: Power
blocks.role: Two 18650 cells in a holder with protection and a power switch, stepped down to 3.3 V for the controller; cells are removed and charged in an external charger.
blocks.parts: 2 x protected 18650, 2S holder, 2S BMS board, 3.3 V buck regulator (e.g. MP1584 module)

blocks.name: Controller
blocks.role: Receives drive commands from the phone over Wi-Fi/Bluetooth and sets motor speed and direction.

blocks.name: Motor driver
blocks.role: Switches battery power to the two motors forward and reverse with PWM speed control.

blocks.name: Motors and wheels
blocks.role: Two geared DC motors drive the wheels; steering is done by running them at different speeds.
blocks.parts: 2 x N20 6 V metal gear motors (about 200 RPM) with 43 mm wheels, ball caster

blocks.name: Chassis
blocks.role: Holds the motors, battery and electronics.
blocks.parts: Off-the-shelf 2WD acrylic chassis kit or 3D-printed plate

risks: The idea is very open: if you meant an arm, walker or something else, the motors, driver and cost change completely. Confirm the robot type first.
Motor start-up current can dip the supply and reset the controller. Add a bulk capacitor (470 uF or more) at the driver and check the 3.3 V rail under stall.
Lithium cells can be damaged or dangerous if shorted or over-discharged. Use protected cells or a BMS, and add a fuse.
A fresh 2S pack (8.4 V) exceeds the 6 V motor rating. Limit PWM duty in firmware to keep the average voltage at or below 6 V.

zones.name: Battery pack, protection, switch and 3.3 V buck

product.name: Desktop 2WD phone-controlled rover
product.summary: Note: the user picked 'walking robot', but every requirement and block in the brief still describes a two-wheel-plus-caster rover, so this layout follows the wheeled requirements; a walker would need servos and a different split. A 3D-printed PETG deck plate carries two N20 gear motors with 43 mm wheels and a ball caster underneath, and the 2S 18650 pack, 3.3 V buck, ESP32-C3 controller and DRV8833 driver on top under a snap-on cover. Scale reference is the 18650 cell (18 x 65 mm) and the 43 mm wheels; everything is assumed, nothing observed.
product.powerInput: 2 x protected 18650 in series, 6.0-8.4 V (7.4 V nominal), about 3 A peak; cells removed for external charging

parts.name: Chassis deck plate
parts.function: Structural base that carries the battery and controller on top and the motors and caster underneath.
parts.process: FDM 3D printing, printed flat with top face on the bed or with pylons up
parts.evidence: Brief: 110 x 166 x 3 mm PETG plate, underside at Z=+6, top face at Z=+9.
parts.unknowns: Final hole patterns for board and battery holder must be confirmed against the control and power sub-assemblies before printing.

parts.name: Snap-on top cover
parts.function: Encloses the battery, buck converter and controller, and carries the switch, USB-C and LED openings.
parts.process: FDM 3D printing, printed top face down
parts.evidence: Brief: 2 mm wall PETG shell about 110 x 166 x 29 mm, open face down, top at Z=+38.
parts.unknowns: Internal clearance over the 18650 holder (about 20 mm tall on the deck) leaves about 7 mm; check against the real holder.

parts.name: Cover corner screw boss
parts.function: Receives the M3 self-tapping screw that clamps the cover to the deck.
parts.process: Printed as one piece with the cover
parts.evidence: Brief: four M3 x 8 self-tapping screws into corner bosses. Placed in the cover's inside corners, Z=+9 to +19, with a 2.5 mm pilot hole.
parts.unknowns: The corners graze the edges of the power and control boxes; check that the battery holder and board corners clear a 7 mm boss.

parts.name: M3 x 8 self-tapping screw, countersunk
parts.function: Holds the cover to the deck; inserted from below with the head flush in the 3 mm deck.
parts.package: M3 x 8 countersunk, thread-forming for plastic
parts.evidence: Brief: four M3 x 8 self-tapping screws. Countersunk from the deck underside so nothing protrudes below Z=+6.

parts.name: Motor pylon
parts.function: Drops the N20 motor bracket mounting face to Z=-11.5 so the 43 mm wheels sit at the correct height.
parts.process: Printed as one piece with the deck
parts.evidence: Brief: pylons at X=+/-38, Y=-30 from the deck underside (Z=+6) to Z=-11.5, with two M2 holes 18 mm apart along Y.
parts.unknowns: Confirm the Pololu N20 bracket hole spacing (18 mm) and the wheel axle height with the drive sub-assembly.

parts.name: M2 pilot hole in pylon face
parts.function: Takes the M2 screw of the N20 motor bracket.
parts.evidence: Brief: two M2 holes per pylon, 18 mm apart along Y, at Y=-39 and Y=-21. Modelled as 1.7 mm pilot holes 6 mm deep.
parts.unknowns: M2 heat-set inserts could replace the pilot holes if the brackets will be removed often.

parts.name: Caster pedestal
parts.function: Drops the ball caster mounting face to Z=-15 so the rover sits level on three points.
parts.process: Printed as one piece with the deck
parts.evidence: Brief: pedestal at X=0, Y=+65 from the deck underside to Z=-15, with two M2 holes 13.5 mm apart along X.
parts.unknowns: Pedestal height depends on the actual caster height; adjust so the deck is level with the wheels fitted.

parts.name: M2 pilot hole in pedestal face
parts.function: Takes the M2 screw of the ball caster.
parts.evidence: Brief: two M2 holes 13.5 mm apart along X, at X=+/-6.75.

parts.name: Motor wire slot
parts.function: Lets each motor lead pair with its JST-XH plug pass up through the deck to the driver.
parts.evidence: Brief: two 10 x 5 mm slots through the deck at X=+/-20, Y=-30. A JST-XH 2-pin housing (about 7.4 x 5.8 mm) passes if fed end-on.
parts.unknowns: A JST-XH plug is 5.8 mm thick, so the 5 mm slot may need widening to 6.5 mm, or the plug must be crimped after routing.

parts.name: M2.5 controller standoff boss
parts.function: Raises the controller board 4 mm off the deck and takes its M2.5 screws.
parts.process: Printed as one piece with the deck
parts.evidence: Brief: four M2.5 standoff bosses on the front half of the deck. Placed on an assumed 60 x 50 mm pattern centred at Y=-40; 4 mm height puts a 1.6 mm board's USB-C centre near Z=+16.
parts.unknowns: The 60 x 50 mm hole pattern is a placeholder; take the real pattern from the control sub-assembly.

parts.name: M3 battery holder hole
parts.function: Through-hole for the M3 screw that fixes the 2S 18650 holder to the deck.
parts.evidence: Brief: two M3 holes in the rear half. Placed at X=+/-20, Y=+44, the centre of the power box; 3.2 mm clearance diameter.
parts.unknowns: Hole positions must match the holder chosen by the power sub-assembly. Screw heads or nuts must be countersunk or captive so nothing sits below Z=+6.

parts.name: Rocker switch cut-out
parts.function: Opening in the rear wall that the power rocker switch snaps into.
parts.evidence: Brief: 19.5 x 13 mm cut-out in the rear wall (Y=+83) centred at X=0, Z=+24.
parts.unknowns: Snap-in rockers of this size are specified for 0.75 to 2 mm panels, so the 2 mm wall is at the limit; check the switch datasheet.

parts.name: USB-C access slot
parts.function: Opening in the front wall for plugging a USB-C cable into the controller for programming.
parts.evidence: Brief: 10 x 4 mm slot in the front wall at X=-20, Z=+16.
parts.unknowns: A USB-C plug overmould is about 12 x 6.5 mm, so the slot only works if the receptacle sits flush with the wall; otherwise enlarge it to 13 x 7 mm.

parts.name: Status LED light-pipe hole
parts.function: Lets the status and low-battery LED be seen from above, optionally through a 3 mm clear light pipe.
parts.evidence: Brief: 3 mm hole in the cover top at X=30, Y=-60.
parts.unknowns: The LED must sit under X=30, Y=-60 on the controller board; confirm with the control sub-assembly.

parts.name: Left N20 gear motor, 6 V 100:1
parts.function: Drives the left wheel at about 200 RPM no-load from the left H-bridge output.
parts.material: Steel can, brass gearbox plates, steel D-shaft
parts.package: N20 micro metal gearmotor, 3 mm D-shaft
parts.evidence: Brief specifies N20 6 V metal gear motor, axis along X, shaft outward, axle at Y=-30, Z=-16.5.
parts.unknowns: Exact ratio and stall current depend on the motor bought; measure stall current at 6 V before trusting the 1.5 A figure.

parts.name: Right N20 gear motor, 6 V 100:1
parts.function: Drives the right wheel at about 200 RPM no-load from the right H-bridge output.
parts.material: Steel can, brass gearbox plates, steel D-shaft
parts.package: N20 micro metal gearmotor, 3 mm D-shaft
parts.evidence: Brief specifies N20 6 V metal gear motor, axis along X, shaft outward, axle at Y=-30, Z=-16.5.
parts.unknowns: Same motor as the left side; it is mounted mirrored, so firmware must invert one direction.

parts.evidence: Brief calls for Pololu #989 extended bracket with two M2 holes 18 mm apart.

parts.name: Right N20 extended motor bracket
parts.function: Clamps the right motor can up against the housing pylon face at Z=-11.5.

parts.name: M2 x 8 pan-head bracket screw
parts.function: Fastens the bracket ears up into the pylon, two per motor at 18 mm spacing.
parts.evidence: Brief: two M2 screws per bracket into the pylon face at Z=-11.5.
parts.unknowns: Whether the pylon takes self-tapped threads in PETG or captive M2 nuts is the housing engineer's choice.

parts.name: Left wheel 43 x 7 mm, 3 mm D-bore
parts.function: Left traction wheel, pressed on the motor D-shaft, touches the ground at Z=-38.
parts.material: Silicone or rubber tyre on ABS hub

parts.evidence: Brief: 43 x 7 mm rubber-tyred D-bore wheel centred at X=-66.

parts.name: 3/4 inch metal ball caster
parts.function: Rear third support point; the ball rolls in any direction and touches the ground at Z=-38.
parts.material: ABS housing, steel ball, roller pins

parts.unknowns: Real height depends on the spacers used; check the deck sits level once the wheels are on, and shim the caster if not.

parts.name: M2 x 8 pan-head caster screw
parts.function: Fastens the caster flange up into the housing pedestal.
parts.evidence: Brief: caster screwed to the pedestal face at Z=-15.
parts.unknowns: The real caster flange hole pattern must be measured and passed to the housing engineer.

parts.name: Left motor suppression capacitor 100 nF
parts.function: Shunts brush noise across the left motor terminals to protect the radio and logic.
parts.package: Radial ceramic disc or MLCC, 50 V
parts.evidence: Brief: 100 nF ceramic soldered across each motor's terminals.

parts.name: Right motor suppression capacitor 100 nF
parts.function: Shunts brush noise across the right motor terminals to protect the radio and logic.
parts.package: Radial ceramic disc or MLCC, 50 V
parts.evidence: Brief: 100 nF ceramic soldered across each motor's terminals.

parts.name: Left motor lead pair, 26 AWG
parts.function: Carries the left H-bridge output from the plug down to the motor terminals.
parts.material: PVC-insulated stranded copper, red and black
parts.evidence: Brief: 2-wire 26 AWG pair from each motor up through the deck slot at X=-20, Y=-30.
parts.unknowns: Only the under-deck run is modelled; cut the pair about 120 mm long so it reaches the driver board.

parts.name: Right motor lead pair, 26 AWG
parts.function: Carries the right H-bridge output from the plug down to the motor terminals.
parts.material: PVC-insulated stranded copper, red and black
parts.evidence: Brief: 2-wire 26 AWG pair from each motor up through the deck slot at X=+20, Y=-30.
parts.unknowns: Only the under-deck run is modelled; cut the pair about 120 mm long so it reaches the driver board.

parts.name: Left JST-XH 2-pin plug
parts.function: Plugs the left motor pair into the driver's left output header.
parts.package: JST XHP-2 housing, 2.5 mm pitch, crimp contacts
parts.evidence: Brief: leads end in 2-pin JST-XH plugs at the deck slots.
parts.unknowns: Shown parked just below the slot to stay in the drive box; in the finished rover it is fed through the slot to the driver. The slot must clear 7.4 x 5.8 mm.

parts.name: Right JST-XH 2-pin plug
parts.function: Plugs the right motor pair into the driver's right output header.
parts.package: JST XHP-2 housing, 2.5 mm pitch, crimp contacts
parts.evidence: Brief: leads end in 2-pin JST-XH plugs at the deck slots.
parts.unknowns: Shown parked just below the slot to stay in the drive box; in the finished rover it is fed through the slot to the driver. The slot must clear 7.4 x 5.8 mm.

parts.name: 2-cell series 18650 holder (Keystone 1049 style)
parts.function: Holds the two 18650 cells in series and bolts the pack to the deck.
parts.material: Glass-filled nylon or PP with nickel-plated spring steel contacts
candidates: generic 2x18650 series holder with solder lugs
parts.evidence: Brief calls for a Keystone 1049 style 77 x 41 x 21 mm holder. Moved back to Y=43 (brief said 38) so the buck module fits in front of it inside the power box.
parts.unknowns: Exact mounting hole spacing and whether protected 69 mm cells fit the chosen holder; check the datasheet before printing the deck.

parts.name: Protected 18650 Li-ion cell
parts.function: Stores energy; two in series give 6.0 to 8.4 V, about 2.5 Ah.
parts.evidence: Brief: two protected 18650 cells, 18.5 x 69 mm, axes along X.
parts.unknowns: Real capacity and whether the cell PCM plus the pack BMS trip in a sensible order; measure trip current.

parts.name: M3 x 8 countersunk screw
parts.function: Fixes the battery holder to the deck.
parts.evidence: Brief: two M3 countersunk screws into the deck; only the heads lie inside the power box, threads go into the deck.
parts.unknowns: Hole positions must match the holder actually bought.

parts.name: 2S 8.4 V BMS board
parts.function: Protects the pack against over-charge, over-discharge and short circuit.
parts.package: Bare PCB with pads B+, BM, B-, P+, P-
candidates: generic 2S BMS with DW01-type protector and dual MOSFETs
parts.evidence: Brief: HX-2S-JH20 style 36 x 7 x 3 mm board taped to the holder front; stands on edge, shifted to X=+10 to clear the buck module.
parts.unknowns: Actual over-current trip point (nominally 10 A); the 2 A fuse should blow first on a sustained fault.

parts.name: Inline mini blade fuse holder with 2 A fuse
parts.function: Fuses the positive lead between BMS and switch.
candidates: Littelfuse MINI 2 A (grey) in inline holder
parts.evidence: Brief: 2 A blade or inline mini fuse in the positive lead; laid on the deck in front of the holder on the right.
parts.unknowns: Two motors stalled (3 A) would blow a 2 A fuse; confirm the controller limits current or choose 3 A.

parts.name: SPST rocker switch
parts.function: Main on/off switch in the positive lead, snapped into the cover's rear wall.
parts.package: Snap-in panel mount, 2 x 4.8 mm tabs
parts.evidence: Brief: KCD1-101 in a 19.5 x 13 mm cut-out at X=0, Y=+83, Z=+24; the bezel face sits at the rear wall.
parts.unknowns: Only 0.5 mm clearance to the holder's rear face; check terminal length or use right-angle crimp tabs.

parts.name: MP1584EN buck module, set to 3.3 V
parts.function: Steps switched battery voltage down to 3.3 V at up to 1 A for the controller.
parts.evidence: Brief: 22 x 17 x 4 mm module at X=-30; placed at Y=13.7 instead of 10 so it stays inside the power box.
parts.unknowns: Set the trimmer to 3.30 V and glue it before connecting the controller; verify ripple under Wi-Fi bursts.

parts.name: Double-sided foam tape pad
parts.function: Sticks the buck module to the deck and insulates its underside.
parts.evidence: Brief: buck module on double-sided foam tape.

parts.name: Battery harness, 22 AWG red/black
parts.function: Carries pack positive from fuse to switch and back to the buck, plus ground, along the right side of the holder.
parts.evidence: Brief: 22 AWG red/black wiring in series after the BMS; routed in the gap beside the holder.
parts.unknowns: Exact routing; add a cable tie point on the deck.

parts.name: 3-pin JST-XH output lead (VBAT, 3V3, GND)
parts.function: Hands switched VBAT, 3.3 V and ground to the control board.
parts.evidence: Brief: 3-pin JST-XH lead about 80 mm long toward the front; shown folded at the front edge of the power box, to be pulled forward to Y=0 and beyond.
parts.unknowns: Pin order must be agreed with the control board; mark pin 1 = VBAT.

parts.name: Perfboard carrier 70 x 50 mm
parts.function: Carries the plug-in controller and driver modules, the connectors and the few discrete parts, with point-to-point wiring underneath.
parts.process: Cut from stock perfboard, hand soldered
parts.evidence: Brief: 70 x 50 x 1.6 mm FR-4 perfboard centred at X=0, Y=-42 on 6 mm standoffs above the deck face at Z=+9.
parts.unknowns: Mounting hole pattern chosen here is 65 x 45 mm (holes at X=+/-32.5, Y=-64.5 and -19.5); housing must match its bosses to this.

parts.name: M2.5 x 6 mm hex standoff
parts.function: Lifts the perfboard 6 mm off the deck so solder joints and wiring clear the PETG.
parts.evidence: Brief: four 6 mm M2.5 standoffs on housing bosses.
parts.unknowns: Nylon standoffs would also work; male stud length must suit the deck boss depth.

parts.name: M2.5 x 5 pan head screw
parts.function: Clamps the perfboard to the standoffs.
parts.evidence: Follows from the M2.5 standoff mounting in the brief.

parts.name: 1x15 female header 2.54 mm (ESP32 socket)
parts.function: Socket rows that let the ESP32-C3 dev board plug in and out of the carrier.
parts.evidence: Brief: female 2.54 mm headers carrying the dev board; DevKitM-1 rows are 22.86 mm apart.
parts.unknowns: Confirm the 22.86 mm row spacing against the actual dev board before soldering.

parts.name: ESP32-C3-DevKitM-1 board
parts.function: Controller board that hosts the radio module, USB-C programming port and USB-UART bridge.
parts.package: 39 x 25.4 mm dev board, 2 x 15 pin headers
parts.evidence: Brief names the Espressif ESP32-C3-DevKitM-1, 39 x 25.4 mm, at X=-20 with USB-C toward the front wall.
parts.unknowns: On the real DevKitM-1 the antenna is at the end opposite the USB-C port, so with USB facing front the antenna faces the rear (Y about -23), not the front edge as the brief says. It is still about 28 mm from the battery pack; keep motor and power leads away from it. USB-C face sits at Y=-62, about 20 mm behind the front wall, so the housing slot must admit the plug overmould.

parts.name: ESP32-C3-MINI-1 module (shield can)
parts.function: RISC-V MCU with Wi-Fi/BLE that generates the motor PWM, reads battery voltage and talks to the phone.
parts.evidence: The DevKitM-1 carries an ESP32-C3-MINI-1 module.
parts.unknowns: Pin plan proposed: GPIO4/5/6/7 PWM, GPIO10 nSLEEP, GPIO3 ADC, GPIO0/1 LED. Strapping pins 2, 8 and 9 are avoided.

parts.name: Module PCB antenna
parts.function: Radiates the 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi/BLE link to the phone.
parts.evidence: ESP32-C3-MINI-1 has an inverted-F PCB trace antenna at one end of the module.
parts.unknowns: Left motor JST and its lead sit about 6 mm below the antenna; if range is poor, route that lead straight down the slot or move the header outboard.

parts.name: 1x8 female header 2.54 mm (driver socket)
parts.function: Socket rows for the DRV8833 carrier.
parts.evidence: Brief: female headers carrying the driver breakout; Pololu #2130 rows are 10.16 mm apart.

parts.name: DRV8833 dual H-bridge carrier
parts.function: Drives the two N20 motors forward/reverse from four PWM inputs, with current limit and thermal shutdown.
parts.evidence: Brief names Pololu #2130, 12.7 x 20 mm, 1.2 A continuous per channel.
parts.unknowns: N20 stall (about 1.5 A) exceeds 1.2 A continuous; the chip will current-limit or thermally trip on a long stall. Firmware should cut drive on a stall timeout.

parts.name: 470 uF 16 V electrolytic
parts.function: Local VBAT reservoir at the driver that absorbs PWM ripple and motor start surges.
parts.evidence: Brief: 470 uF 16 V electrolytic across VBAT at the driver.

parts.name: JST-XH 3-pin header (power in)
parts.function: Receives switched VBAT, 3.3 V and ground from the power sub-assembly lead.
parts.evidence: Brief: 3-pin JST-XH for the power lead at the board's rear edge.
parts.unknowns: Pin order (VBAT, GND, 3V3) must be agreed with the power lead; XH is 2.5 mm pitch, so pins need a slight tweak on 2.54 mm perfboard.

parts.name: JST-XH 2-pin header (motor out)
parts.function: Motor output connectors for the left and right N20 leads coming up through the deck slots.
parts.evidence: Brief: two 2-pin JST-XH headers at X=+/-20 on the rear edge.
parts.unknowns: Left header is J4 (AOUT), right is J5 (BOUT). Motor polarity is fixed in firmware after a first spin test.

parts.name: 3V3 isolation jumper
parts.function: Disconnects the external 3.3 V buck from the dev board while it is powered from USB, so the two supplies never fight.
parts.evidence: Added because the DevKitM-1 has its own 5 V to 3.3 V LDO on the same 3V3 pin that the buck feeds.
parts.unknowns: Not in the brief. Alternative is simply never plugging USB with the pack switched on.

parts.name: Battery divider resistors 100k / 33k
parts.function: Scales VBAT by 0.248 so 8.4 V reads 2.08 V and the 6.4 V cut-off reads 1.59 V at the ADC.
parts.evidence: Brief: 100k/33k divider from VBAT to an ADC pin.
parts.unknowns: R1 is 100k (top), R2 is 33k (bottom). Use ADC attenuation 11 dB and calibrate against a multimeter.

parts.name: 100 nF ADC filter capacitor
parts.function: Filters motor PWM noise on the divider tap and gives the ADC a low-impedance sample source.
parts.package: Radial MLCC, 5 mm pitch, X7R 50 V
parts.evidence: Brief: 100 nF capacitor on the divider.

parts.name: 3 mm red/green bi-colour LED
parts.function: Shows green for link/ready and red for low battery under the cover light pipe.
parts.evidence: Brief: 3 mm red/green status LED at X=30, Y=-60.
parts.unknowns: LED tip is at Z=24.6; the housing light pipe must reach down to about there.

parts.name: LED resistors 330 ohm
parts.function: Set about 3 to 4 mA through each LED colour from a 3.3 V GPIO.
parts.evidence: Brief: 330 ohm resistors for the status LED.

unknowns: Product type: the user picked 'walking robot' but the brief describes a wheeled rover; confirm which is wanted before printing.

Standoff stack: housing gives 4 mm printed bosses, control adds 6 mm hex standoffs. Decide whether both are used (10 mm total) and check cover clearance above the ESP32 dev board and the 470 uF capacitor.
JST-XH 3-pin pin order (VBAT, 3V3, GND) must match on the lead and on J3; a swap would put 8.4 V on the 3.3 V rail.
Fuse margin: two motors stalled at 1.5 A each exceed the 2 A fuse and may also trip the BMS. Confirm actual N20 stall current at 8.4 V, or limit duty in firmware.
6 V motors on a 2S pack: PWM duty should be capped at about 70 percent at full charge; not yet defined in firmware.
Motor polarity at each plug is not fixed; one side may run backwards until swapped in the plug or in firmware.
No charging path is defined: cells are assumed to be removed for an external charger, or a 2S charger input needs adding.
Phone control is all in the app over Wi-Fi/BLE; app commands and LED colour meanings are firmware decisions not yet set.
Whether the cover material and battery position detune the module PCB antenna; range is untested.
verifySteps: Before plugging in the control board, switch on and measure the power lead: pin 1 6.0-8.4 V, pin 2 3.30 V, pin 3 ground. Adjust the MP1584 trimmer if needed.
Check continuity of the JST-XH pin order against J3 on the perfboard.
Measure each motor's stall current at 8.4 V with a bench supply and compare with the 2 A fuse and DRV8833 limit.
With wheels off the ground, command forward and confirm both wheels turn the same way; swap a plug or firmware sign if not.
Measure the ADC tap at GPIO3: expect about 0.248 x VBAT (2.08 V at 8.4 V).
Scope the 3.3 V rail during motor start and reversal; dips below 3.0 V mean more decoupling or separate routing is needed.
Test-fit: wheel and caster contact points all at Z=-38 on a flat surface, plugs pass through the wire slots, USB-C and LED line up with the cover openings, cover closes over the tallest parts.
Drive it at range and check the Wi-Fi/BLE link with the cover on and off.
safety: Li-ion 18650 cells: a short can cause fire. Use protected cells, keep the BMS and fuse in circuit, never bridge the holder contacts, and observe polarity when inserting cells.
Charge only with a proper 2S (8.4 V) Li-ion charger, attended, and never charge damaged or swollen cells.
Remove JP1 (3V3 jumper) before connecting USB with the battery on, so the buck and the USB regulator do not fight.
A stalled motor heats the motor and the DRV8833; release a jammed wheel promptly and keep fingers and hair away from wheels and gears.
Switch off or remove the cells before working on the wiring; the pack can deliver many amps into a short ahead of the fuse.
PETG softens around 70-80 C: keep the buck and driver from pressing hot against the deck and do not leave the rover in a hot car.

firmware.summary: The rover starts its own Wi-Fi access point and serves a touch-joystick page at http://192.168.4.1; the phone sends throttle and turn about ten times a second. The firmware mixes these into left and right wheel speeds and drives the DRV8833 with 20 kHz PWM capped at 75 % duty, with ramping to keep start surges down. If commands stop for 0.5 s, the motors coast and the driver is put to sleep; this failsafe runs in its own 10 ms task, so a stalled web request cannot delay it. Battery voltage is read through the 100k/33k divider on GPIO3: below 6.8 V the red LED flashes, and below 6.4 V for 2 s the motors lock out until the pack is back above 7.0 V. Green blinks while waiting for the phone and is solid while it is driving.

#pragma once
// Pin map, matches the design's connections.
// Strapping pins GPIO2, GPIO8 and GPIO9 are deliberately left unused.

#define PIN_LED_GREEN   0   // D1 green anode via R3 330R, active high
#define PIN_LED_RED     1   // D1 red anode via R3 330R, active high
#define PIN_VBAT_SENSE  3   // ADC1_CH3, 100k/33k divider tap + 100 nF
#define PIN_AIN1        4   // DRV8833 AIN1 (left motor forward)
#define PIN_AIN2        5   // DRV8833 AIN2 (left motor reverse)
#define PIN_BIN1        6   // DRV8833 BIN1 (right motor forward)
#define PIN_BIN2        7   // DRV8833 BIN2 (right motor reverse)
#define PIN_NSLEEP      10  // DRV8833 nSLEEP, low = outputs off

#pragma once
#include <stdint.h>

// ---- Wi-Fi access point (change the password before use) ----
#define AP_SSID_PREFIX   "Rover-"
#define AP_PASSWORD      "rover1234"   // WPA2 needs at least 8 characters
#define AP_CHANNEL       6
#define AP_MAX_CLIENTS   1             // only one phone may drive at a time

// ---- Motor PWM ----
#define PWM_FREQ_HZ      20000
#define PWM_BITS         10
#define PWM_FULL         1023
#define DUTY_MAX         767           // 75 % cap: 8.4 V pack -> about 6.3 V on a 6 V motor
#define DUTY_MIN         205           // 20 %: roughly where an N20 starts to turn
#define CMD_DEADBAND     5             // commands under 5 % count as stop
#define TURN_GAIN_PCT    70            // tames steering so the rover is not twitchy
#define INVERT_LEFT      false         // flip if a wheel runs backwards
#define INVERT_RIGHT     false

// ---- Control loop ----
#define CONTROL_PERIOD_MS  10
#define CMD_TIMEOUT_MS     500         // motors stop if no command for this long
#define ACCEL_STEP         4           // % per tick: 0 -> 100 % in 250 ms, limits start surge
#define DECEL_STEP         10          // % per tick: 100 -> 0 % in 100 ms

// ---- Battery (2S Li-ion through 100k / 33k divider) ----
#define DIV_R_TOP_K        100
#define DIV_R_BOTTOM_K     33
#define VBAT_CAL_PERMILLE  1000        // trim after comparing with a multimeter
#define VBAT_WARN_MV       6800        // red LED starts flashing
#define VBAT_CUTOFF_MV     6400        // motors locked out
#define VBAT_RECOVER_MV    7000        // clears warning and lock-out
#define VBAT_CUTOFF_HOLD_MS 2000       // must stay low this long, rides through start sag
#define VBAT_SAMPLE_MS     20

build: Install PlatformIO Core (pip install platformio) or the PlatformIO extension for VS Code.
Put the files in a project folder with the generated platformio.ini, then build with: pio run
Remove the JP1 3V3 jumper before plugging in USB so the buck and the USB regulator never fight, then connect the dev board's USB-C port.
Watch the console with: pio device monitor -b 115200
Unplug USB, refit JP1, and switch the rover on from the rocker switch for battery use.
test: USB only, JP1 removed, battery switch off, wheels off the ground: the console should print 'Rover booting' and a VBAT near 0 mV, the red LED should be solid, and the motors must not move.

Join the Wi-Fi network 'Rover-XXXX' (password rover1234) with a phone and open http://192.168.4.1; the page should show the voltage and 'battery empty, motors locked', and dragging the joystick must not move the wheels.

Still on USB with JP1 removed, switch the battery on with charged cells: within a second the red LED should go out, green should go solid while the page is open, and the page voltage should match a multimeter on J3 pin 1 within about 0.1 V (trim VBAT_CAL_PERMILLE in config.h if not).
With the wheels still off the ground, push the joystick slightly forward: both wheels should turn forward slowly. If one runs backwards, set INVERT_LEFT or INVERT_RIGHT, or swap that motor's plug.
Push the joystick right: the left wheel should run faster than the right; at full right with no throttle the wheels should counter-rotate.
Scope or meter AIN1 (GPIO4) at full forward: 20 kHz with duty no higher than 75 %.
Failsafe: hold full forward, then turn the phone's Wi-Fi off or close the browser tab. The wheels must stop within about half a second and green should go back to blinking.
Release the joystick: the wheels should stop within about 0.1 s and the knob should re-centre.

Low battery: feed J3 from a bench supply (current limit 1 A) instead of the pack. Drop to 6.7 V: the red LED flashes. Drop to 6.3 V for more than 2 s: red goes solid and the motors stop. Raise above 7.0 V: back to green and drivable.
Finally, refit JP1, unplug USB, put the rover on the floor and drive gently; check that the 2 A fuse holds during quick reversals.
assumptions: The brief's 'walking robot' label is ignored, as the design notes say; this firmware is for the two-wheel rover that the parts and connections describe.
The design only says 'phone-controlled' over Wi-Fi/BLE. I chose a Wi-Fi access point with a built-in web joystick so no phone app or extra library is needed; BLE is not used.
The AP is 'Rover-' plus the last two MAC bytes, password 'rover1234', channel 6, at 192.168.4.1, limited to one client. Change the password in config.h.
Control uses plain HTTP GET /d?x=&y= at about 10 Hz (x = turn, y = throttle, -100..100), not WebSocket; the reply carries battery voltage and state.
Motors coast and the DRV8833 is put to sleep if no command arrives for 500 ms.

DRV8833 channel A (AIN1/AIN2, GPIO4/5) is the left motor and channel B (BIN1/BIN2, GPIO6/7) is the right; the design does not say which is which. INVERT_LEFT / INVERT_RIGHT in config.h fix wiring polarity.

Drive is fast decay (one input PWM, the other low), so every input low means coast. PWM is 20 kHz, 10-bit, hard-capped at 75 % duty as the design states; the cap is fixed and not compensated for battery voltage.
Minimum running duty is 20 % and the joystick deadband is 5 %; both are guesses for N20 100:1 motors and can be tuned in config.h.
Ramp is 0 to full in 250 ms and full to 0 in 100 ms, to keep two motors' start current under the 2 A fuse. Turn gain is 70 %.

The Pololu DRV8833 carrier pulls nSLEEP high on its own, so the driver is awake for the few milliseconds before the firmware runs; its inputs have internal pull-downs, so the motors coast in that window.
Battery thresholds: warning at 6.8 V, cut-off at 6.4 V (from the design) held for 2 s to ride through motor sag, recovery at 7.0 V. The warning and recovery levels and the hold time are my choices.
Battery reading uses the ESP32-C3 factory ADC calibration (analogReadMilliVolts) at 11 dB attenuation and the nominal 100k/33k ratio, with a trim constant in config.h.
At cut-off the firmware only locks the motors and shows red; it does not deep-sleep. The 2S BMS is relied on for final over-discharge protection.
With no battery (USB only) VBAT reads about 0 V, so the motors stay locked and the LED is solid red; this is intended.

LED meanings: green blinking = ready and waiting for the phone, green solid = commands arriving, red flashing = low battery, red solid = cut-off. The design only says green for link/ready and red for low battery.
The serial console is 115200 baud on the dev board's USB-UART bridge (UART0); GPIO20/21 are left to it. Strapping pins GPIO2, GPIO8 and GPIO9 are unused.
No task watchdog is enabled. The failsafe relies on the 10 ms control task, which runs at higher priority than the web server loop.
Platform is pinned to espressif32@6.9.0 (Arduino core 2.0.x); the PWM code also compiles against core 3.x. No external libraries are used.
Nothing here has been compiled or run on hardware; treat the bench tests as the first real check.

controls.label: Power
controls.action: Connects the fused battery to the buck and motor driver, so the controller boots, the status LED lights and the motors can respond to the phone.

unknowns: Product type: the user picked 'walking robot' but the brief describes a wheeled rover; confirm which is wanted before printing.

Standoff stack: housing gives 4 mm printed bosses, control adds 6 mm hex standoffs. Decide whether both are used (10 mm total) and check cover clearance above the ESP32 dev board and the 470 uF capacitor.
JST-XH 3-pin pin order (VBAT, 3V3, GND) must match on the lead and on J3; a swap would put 8.4 V on the 3.3 V rail.
Fuse margin: two motors stalled at 1.5 A each exceed the 2 A fuse and may also trip the BMS. Confirm actual N20 stall current at 8.4 V, or limit duty in firmware.
6 V motors on a 2S pack: PWM duty should be capped at about 70 percent at full charge; not yet defined in firmware.
Motor polarity at each plug is not fixed; one side may run backwards until swapped in the plug or in firmware.
No charging path is defined: cells are assumed to be removed for an external charger, or a 2S charger input needs adding.
Phone control is all in the app over Wi-Fi/BLE; app commands and LED colour meanings are firmware decisions not yet set.
Whether the cover material and battery position detune the module PCB antenna; range is untested.
verifySteps: Before plugging in the control board, switch on and measure the power lead: pin 1 6.0-8.4 V, pin 2 3.30 V, pin 3 ground. Adjust the MP1584 trimmer if needed.
Check continuity of the JST-XH pin order against J3 on the perfboard.
Measure each motor's stall current at 8.4 V with a bench supply and compare with the 2 A fuse and DRV8833 limit.
With wheels off the ground, command forward and confirm both wheels turn the same way; swap a plug or firmware sign if not.
Measure the ADC tap at GPIO3: expect about 0.248 x VBAT (2.08 V at 8.4 V).
Scope the 3.3 V rail during motor start and reversal; dips below 3.0 V mean more decoupling or separate routing is needed.
Test-fit: wheel and caster contact points all at Z=-38 on a flat surface, plugs pass through the wire slots, USB-C and LED line up with the cover openings, cover closes over the tallest parts.
Drive it at range and check the Wi-Fi/BLE link with the cover on and off.
safety: Li-ion 18650 cells: a short can cause fire. Use protected cells, keep the BMS and fuse in circuit, never bridge the holder contacts, and observe polarity when inserting cells.
Charge only with a proper 2S (8.4 V) Li-ion charger, attended, and never charge damaged or swollen cells.
Remove JP1 (3V3 jumper) before connecting USB with the battery on, so the buck and the USB regulator do not fight.
A stalled motor heats the motor and the DRV8833; release a jammed wheel promptly and keep fingers and hair away from wheels and gears.
Switch off or remove the cells before working on the wiring; the pack can deliver many amps into a short ahead of the fuse.
PETG softens around 70-80 C: keep the buck and driver from pressing hot against the deck and do not leave the rover in a hot car.
